title: Jars and envelopes: cash you can see
description: Dividing cash into labelled envelopes is an old method that survives every app — because running out is something you can see and feel.

body.heading: The method in one minute
paragraphs: At the start of the week or month, withdraw a set amount of cash for one flexible category — groceries, eating out, fun — and put it in a labelled envelope or jar. Spend that category only from the envelope. When it is empty, the category is done until the next refill.
No apps, no tracking, no sums. The envelope is simultaneously the budget, the record, and the alarm bell. A thinning envelope on Wednesday tells you more, faster, than any chart.

body.heading: Choose one category, not your whole life
paragraphs: Cash envelopes work best for the categories that leak: food extras, treats, small outings. Rent and bills are usually better handled digitally, where records and automation help.
Pick your leakiest category and run the envelope for a month. Most people find the physical pause — opening the envelope, seeing what remains — changes decisions more than any number on a screen.

body.heading: Digital versions count too
paragraphs: If cash is impractical, many banks offer separate pots or sub-accounts that work the same way: labelled, limited, visible. The technology matters less than the two ingredients — a boundary you can see, and a category with a genuine end.
Whichever form you use, refill on a schedule and resist mid-period top-ups. The moment an empty envelope can be quietly refilled from elsewhere, it stops being a boundary and becomes a suggestion.

takeaway: Give your leakiest spending category a labelled envelope with a fixed amount of cash. When you can see the money leaving, you spend it like it matters.
